title: CLEAR: Cross-Source Evidence Adjudication for Large Language Models in Medicine
research_question: Can an LLM improve medical reasoning by keeping parametric, curated-local, and dynamically retrieved evidence separate, explicitly adjudicating disagreements among them, and selectively performing additional retrieval when existing evidence remains unresolved?
methodology: CLEAR independently produces candidate answers from parametric knowledge, a locally curated corpus, and dynamically retrieved evidence, retaining source-specific evidence and provenance for each pathway. An aggregation verifier examines the candidates together with evidence, provenance, and source-quality signals such as authority, recency, and content type, after which override-guard and challenge-audit mechanisms decide whether to preserve or revise the current conclusion. Unresolved disagreement can trigger a targeted, bounded follow-up query followed by re-adjudication rather than unrestricted search. The framework is evaluated with o3-mini and Qwen-3.5-9B across ten public medical benchmarks, with ablations for evidence-source combinations and follow-up retrieval.

key_findings.finding: CLEAR shows its largest gains when the backbone's parametric baseline is weaker; for Qwen-3.5-9B, the best reported CLEAR configurations substantially improve MedQA and NEJM-QA over direct inference and conventional retrieval baselines.
key_findings.section: 3.1 Results on MCQ Datasets and 4.1 Main Findings

key_findings.finding: For o3-mini across MedQA, PubMedQA, and NEJM-QA, the full three-source CLEAR configuration has the highest aggregate score even though the best individual method varies by dataset.
Targeted follow-up retrieval on Qwen-3.5-9B increases aggregate performance from 77.22 to 78.13, while only 12 of 123 triggered follow-up searches produce an accepted answer revision.

External retrieval is not uniformly beneficial: when the o3-mini parametric baseline is already strong, additional evidence can provide little benefit and the default CLEAR configuration degrades performance on HealthBench.

The architecture preserves the identity and provenance of parametric, local, and dynamic evidence until adjudication, making cross-source agreement and conflict explicit instead of merging all retrieved context before reasoning.

The dynamic-evidence override guard requires relevance, credible sourcing, explicit support, and an explanation of why the competing conclusion is less appropriate before dynamic evidence is allowed to overturn stronger existing conclusions.
The framework's source-quality assessment explicitly permits recency to influence evaluation of dynamically retrieved evidence, providing a mechanism for time-sensitive evidence adjudication.

limitations: All evaluations are offline benchmark studies and do not establish clinical effectiveness, patient safety, or readiness for deployment.
Public medical benchmarks may overlap with model pretraining or post-training data, and the authors cannot fully rule out parametric memorization.
Dynamic web evidence can vary over time, complicating provenance stability and exact reproducibility.

Institutional access restrictions, privacy requirements, and data governance are identified as deployment issues but are not implemented or empirically evaluated as permission-aware controller constraints.
The adjudication logic is substantially prompt- and rule-driven and may itself be sensitive to model post-training behavior.
Broader validation is needed across backbone families, retrievers, search systems, and application domains.
The framework tracks source provenance and recency but does not present a formal version model for mutable documents or a statistical bounded-risk guarantee for stopping follow-up retrieval.
The verifier's confidence output is an operational judgment rather than a demonstrated calibrated probability of correctness.
raw_claims: CLEAR keeps parametric, local-corpus, and dynamic-search candidates as separate evidence pathways before aggregation.
Each pathway carries provenance information into the aggregation stage.
Dynamic source quality can depend on authority, recency, and content type.
The aggregation verifier explicitly reasons about agreement and disagreement among source-specific candidates.
A dynamic source is not automatically allowed to override agreement from other pathways merely because it is newer.
Unresolved conflicts can generate a targeted follow-up query and another adjudication round.
Follow-up retrieval is used selectively rather than as an unconditional extra search step.
The reported benefits are larger for the weaker Qwen backbone than for the stronger o3-mini baseline in several tasks.
On some strong-backbone settings, retrieval provides little benefit or lowers performance.
The evaluation uses public multiple-choice and free-text medical benchmarks rather than private patient records.
The paper explicitly identifies changing search results and external-source reproducibility as deployment concerns.
